newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian economy expands by 8.2 pct in Q1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian economy expands by 8.2 pct in Q1.

text.p: Malaysia's economy expanded 8.2 percent in the first quarter of 1997, but an easing in growth from last year has raised speculation the economy was enjoying a "soft landing".

The central Bank Negara Malaysia said on Friday the 8.2 percent year-on-year figure for the January to March period matched growth in the preceding quarter but was a shade below 8.3 percent in the same quarter in 1996.

"It is a comforting thought that the economy is moving along at around eight percent as opposed to nine percent, which means that the soft landing has been achieved," said Stephen Weller, director of strategy at brokers Pesaka Jardine Fleming in Kuala Lumpur.

Although the figure was at the high end of market forecasts it was well within official targets for full-year growth and local financial markets hardly responded, economists said. "Bank Negara Malaysia's 1997 year-end forecast is eight percent," said research firm MMS International.
In its quarterly report on the economy, the central bank said output in the manufacturing sector grew 12.9 percent, moderating from 13.9 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
Analysts were divided on the possibility of an interest rate cut in Malaysia following the release of the figures.

"The manufacturing growth is more likely to dictate interest rate movements in the near-term," said Weller. "It is showing good growth, but it is down about one percent. This leaves room for an interest rate cut in the second half of this year."
But Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities in Kuala Lumpur, and MMS said they thought the present monetary policy would remain in place.

"Bank Negara will want to keep monetary policy stable. The factor influencing interest rates this year will be the trade deficit. If it stays around 13.5 billion ringgit ($5.4 billion), there will be no room for any rate cut," said Chew.
The services sector grew by nine percent in the first quarter of 1997, compared to 8.7 percent in the same period in 1996.
